posts.title: Talk Announcement: BJACS
posts.content:
Hi everyone!

I will be giving a talk at the Bristol Junior Algebra and Combinatorics Seminar titled “The Injective Generation Condition”. If there are any mathematicians interested in my Master’ project, come and find me at Fry G.07 next Wednesday, 2:30-3:30pm!

Attached below are the title and abstract, the slides of the talk can be found here.

Title: The Injective Generation Condition

Abstract: Let A be a finite dimensional algebra over an algebraically complete field. Rickard proved that if A satisfy a condition which we call “injective generation”, then the finitistic dimension conjecture holds for A. While the conjecture and its consequences are interesting on their own, the talk will focus on introducing and verifying (if time allows) the injective generation condition of a particular algebra A, with methods introduced by Goodearl, Huisgen-Zimmermann and many others.

posts.title: Graduated and next steps: PhD!
posts.content:
Hi everyone! Despite a few drafts in my notebook which I am still procrastinating to finish, here are some life updates!

Graduated!

I have graduated from the University of Bristol, achieving a First Class Honours in MSci Mathematics with Study Abroad!

I want to thank everyone for the support, fun times and laughter in 4 years of my undergraduate life! I enjoyed it very much.

Next Steps

I am also thrilled to announce that my journey with mathematics will not stop here. I will continue to do a PhD in Mathematics here in Bristol, supervised by Professor Jeremy Rickard!

I am very grateful that I can continue my journey with mathematics! I hope to discover more, learn more, and tell others about more interesting facts in mathematics. Please look forward to more presentations, writings and updates that will be posted on this website!

Some Stuff in Summer

While I was on my summer holiday back in Hong Kong from June to August, I also got the chance to teach the Enrichment Programme for Young Mathematics Talents as a teaching assistant. This is a course for talented high school students, hoping they get some hands-on experience with university mathematics. (See the poster attached here.)

I was a TA for the “Towards Differential Geometry” course. During the entire August, I proposed questions for the quizzes and exams, prepared tutorial notes, and taught two 3-hour tutorial sessions. It was a fun experience, and I made a lot of connections with mathematicians and mathematicians-to-be!

And thanks to the enthusiasm of the students, I could be sneaky and talk about some out-of-syllabus materials…! Go to my LinkedIn Profile and see what it is!

What’s next?

I am currently settling down as a PhD Student, joining conferences such as the Heilbronn Annual Conference, and filling out forms to make sure everything is “officially okay”. Oh also, I have an office space now! This is going to be exciting…

posts.title: My Masters Project: The Maths
posts.content:
This post and the next (few, maybe) will be me talking about a project that I did this year. As I have some experience in studying Hong Kong, the UK, and the US, it is very hard to give an official name to this “project”. I mean, it is officially for the “MATHM2200 Project” Unit at the University of Bristol. But some friends called it the “FYP” (stands for “Final Year Project”), and some called it a “Master’s Thesis” or “Final Thesis” (which is technically not the same thing as I am doing an integrated Masters programme…?), and sometimes I simply called it “The Paper” or “The Project”. Anyway, all that is for you to know is I care about this enough to mention it on almost any occasion when I am writing it, so I will talk about it here as well.

This project consists of a report titled “Category Theory and the Injective Generation Condition” and a presentation “Category Theory”. You can find (a draft version of) them in the “Research” section on my website. This post will focus on the maths content more, and the next will be more personal.

Acknowledgement & Disclaimer

A huge thanks to Professor Jeremy Rickard for supervising this project, and a lot of people for their support throughout writing this project, or helping me with the work building up to it. I have an incomplete list of people I want to thank in my acknowledgement section of the paper.

This paper is on Category Theory and Algebras, as much as I want this post to be accessible to a general audience, I recognize that it will be a hard mission to write down adequately, but I will try my best. In other words, undergraduate mathematics students would be most happy with the content of my paper (and the expected level of difficulty for reading the paper anyway).

Part I: Category Theory

My project started as an attempt to understand category theory and its uses in mathematics. At the start of almost any undergraduate mathematics education, students like me will be seeing some kind of “set theory” and how to write proofs with it. Set theory is a basic tool for essentially all mathematicians to form and tackle problems: how many elements are there in a set? If I know two sets A and B, how can one construct functions from A to B? Are they injective and/or surjective (or both, i.e. bijective)? Working with those should be very familiar.

However, as one studies more abstract algebra (a branch of mathematics, it is not the “Algebra” you might be expecting in high school!), one will meet way more structure and their “structure-preserving transformations”. For example:

  • Groups and Group isomorphisms/homomorphisms,
  • Vector spaces and Isomorphic Vector spaces / linear maps,
  • Rings with Ring isomorphism/homomorphism,

(My non-math friends probably will lose it here so early into the passage, I am sorry…) It is quite a lot of definitions to go through, but you can bring one level up in abstraction in category theory!

In category theory, we can start developing it once we define a set (or a “class”, to be precise) of “objects” and “morphisms” satisfying certain conditions. For instance, immediately we have the following categories:

You get the idea. I also tried to present all the basics in the first chapter of my paper. Now I need to try to bring the non-math friends back.

Category Theory enriches (hopefully this is the right word) set theory to allow us to discuss more possibilities in mathematics. I probably cannot say it better than Oliver Lugg’s video. But in my paper, I also mentioned two working principles, which make category theory very versatile.

  1. The idea of duality. Morphisms (or maps) in a category have a source (say A) and a target (say B), but consider maps from A to B, since we just “call them” A and B, the theory makes no difference if we consider maps from B to A. That is, we “say” the “target” is where the maps start and the “source” is where the maps end. We just “say” it is so, so we would not expect the idea would be vastly different. For math people again, this actually tackles a lot of annoying bookkeeping in topics such as dual spaces, left-right module differences, etc.
  2. The idea of universal properties. Sometimes, one might be presented with a mathematical object and don’t know what can be done with it. A good idea is to look at maps coming out / going into this object (and by duality concerns, any of the two would be fine). It turns out that this practice is enough for all practical purposes (the jargon is you can always get the object “up to isomorphism”). An example for the math people again: given two (finite-dimensional) vector spaces V and W, how could we understand the direct sum V+W? Well, one could say if I give you any extra vector space T, and two linear maps f: V to T, and g: W to T, then I can have a “natural” map h: V + W to T (what do you think it is?), this map completely tells me how V+W “behaves”. In fact, the key lemma in Category theory, the Yoneda Lemma, heavily generalizes this observation.

These two concepts made up my second chapter. The third chapter was quite technical, and as I am writing this blog post I feel like it is too inaccessible for the laymen and boring for the mathematicians, so I will not mention it too much. But it involves looking at adjoint functors, which is a way to transport objects between two structurally different categories. The whole first part leads to a nice theorem of “adjoint preserves limits”, but I have no time or space to explain what these words mean.

Part II: Category Theory in Algebras

Anyway, the second part puts category theory into applications in abstract algebra. In particular, I am interested in thinking about modules over non-commutative algebras. Again, the terms “modules”, “non-commutative”, and even “algebra” this time are all technical terms. I don’t know a good way to present it without getting too deep into rewriting the paper, so I would just share my common response when someone asks me what this “algebra” thing is about. For students currently doing their Masters in pure mathematics, you might want to hear that my work also includes some homological algebra.

When I told my friends I was writing a paper, some of them would ask me what is it about. I usually answer “abstract algebra”, and upon further questions, the only words that I manage to spurt out are probably “It is very abstract, I think about how things add and multiply”.

And that’s kinda about it. For the more interested readers, I worked with a special type of algebras called “quiver algebras”, where all the information can be retrieved by drawing a finite directed graph, possibly with multiple edges between two vertices and loops. I was also interested in modules over those algebras. As representation theorists are concerned, the first question is probably to ask for a decomposition of the regular module into indecomposable modules, and there is a nice one consisting of only projective modules.

Back to the normal English language, one thing that was quite unexpected in this project was that I worked a lot with pictures. This is to give a good visualization of different objects. This is also a common theme in both Part I and II of the paper.

In the final chapter, I produced a new calculation, verifying an algebra satisfies a particular condition (injective generation). Combined with my supervisor’s work, this in turn gives an example where a famous conjecture (the “Finitistic Dimension Conjecture”) holds for that algebra.

The Next Post

So that is the math part! Do let me know if you read any part of my paper and have any comments! The next post will be about recounting the writing process, and my experience in battling emotions that arise from it (so it will be much more personal), stay tuned!

posts.title: Summer Research: New Preprint!
posts.content:
Hi everyone! I am announcing a new preprint, “A coarse geometric approach to graph layout problems”, collaborated with Wanying Huang, David Hume, and Samuel J. Kelly from the Summer Research Project at the University of Bristol! I also want to discuss my experience and feelings in mathematics research.

About the Preprint

First, a little bit about the content. This is a research project supervised by Dr David Hume on graph invariants: that is, some integers that we can assign to different graphs. We always work with undirected, connected, but possibly infinite graphs.

A graph is a collection of vertex and edges between them, how can we associate it with a number?

What we are interested in is the growth of a collection of invariants, and it turns out most of them are the “same” when we look at a map of graphs with controlled “expanding” properties (what we call “kappa-regular maps” in our paper.)

I focussed on the discussion of cutwidth, bandwidth, and treewidth, and I have uploaded a separate exposition article titled “Graph Invariants and Regular Maps” here. The exposition is more tailored to undergraduate/talented high school students, by covering only two (Proposition 3.2 and 3.4) in specific cases.

My Experience

A few weeks after the project had ended, I was invited to an internship event and a project presentation, both at the Fry Building at the University of Bristol. As a panelist, I talked more about my personal experience in applying and working on this project at the internship event. I talked more about the subject content and my discoveries in the project presentation. I want to focus on the former more in this post.

I did an 8-week project throughout the summer holiday (from 1 August), and I got an office shared with Sam, Wanying, and another undergraduate student from another project. On the surface, working in research is not the most exciting thing (at least when I type this out I don’t find this particularly exciting): you try to type your own result, working 9-5 Monday to Friday, and you meet with your supervisor weekly to discuss progress and investigate more notes in draft to make sure your work is alright… probably what someone would expect when you are “working in a lab”… I suppose?

However, this doesn’t mean it is not a meaningful experience, I still have a lot of takeaways.

Main Takeaway: Research is Hard.

Although I definitely enjoy committing to reading papers and writing up mathematics, I realized the project put a real test on my mental resilience. At times I have to bang my head on an idea, only to realize it had been proven after an extensive paper search. Sometimes, an idea will not click for me for days, or weeks, even if you spend 8 hours every day looking meticulously at every word in a proof.

That being said, there are some tips and tricks I found useful during these times.

  • Proving very basic properties. When I met a new definition in a paper, I often had a “mental picture” in mind and moved on to read the rest of the paper. But it is good at this time to stop and think about how the new definition fits in with different very basic objects. In my case, consider a graph invariant, what is the invariant on a cycle? A complete graph? A bipartite graph? Working them out could give a hint of how the proof of a general statement may go.
  • Write things down (neater than you thought it might be). It is always a good idea to keep track of your progress. Sometimes when things click, you become so excited (and maybe overly obsessed) with the idea and call it a day because you understand something new. While understanding new things is always a call for celebration, do remember having a record of what you are thinking is always useful (and ultimately, it is what you want to produce at the end of your research). Moreover, there are times (more than I want to admit) where I embarrassed myself by thinking I created a new proof, just to discover that the whole idea breaks down if I write it down formally on LaTex.
  • Talk to others. I feel like this is always highly underrated in research. Making sure I have something to report and ask in my weekly supervisor meeting helps me a lot. But more important than that, talk to your colleagues and friends! When I was presenting a proof to others, I found key insights that I was missing when I was writing alone. Huge shout-outs to Samuel for finding one of the key ideas that I was missing when I was proving a key lemma!
  • Keep yourself active and happy! Doing research is no easy job, and to be fair I still have imposter syndrome lingering in any projects that I did. When I was working on the project, I also always felt like I was embarrassing myself by asking stupid questions and making ridiculous statements every time I met my supervisor. But as time passed, I tried my best to accept this is what research entails, and I have started to enjoy it. In the meantime, I also made sure that I don’t work on Saturdays and Sundays, so I really have time to rest and recharge myself during the weekends. I felt like I really had time to do some stretches, relax, and prepare for next week’s work (definitely not a foreshadowing…)

Final Thank Yous

I want to thank Dr David Hume again for this opportunity and experience, and different people from the School of Mathematics for inviting me to present my experience from both academic and non-academic perspectives! I also want to thank the Bei Shan Tang Foundation for its support through the Lee Hysan Memorial Scholarship for Overseas Studies. This project had been a really good learning experience, I look forward to more mathematical research in the years to come!

posts.title: Coding Club is Back!
posts.content:
I am very happy to announce that the Coding Club, the peer-support session run by Bristol Study Skills is back up and running!

I wrote about my experience with the coding club here, I really enjoyed helping others and am looking forward to helping more students in Bristol this year! Here are the blurb and booking details of the workshop.

The Coding Club

This is a study group for students who are working on coding problems at a beginner to intermediate level. You’re welcome to come whether you’re looking for coding help or to use it as a study space to work on your coding.

This session is for you if:

  • You’re new to programming, or aren’t super confident with working on coding-based problems
  • You have upcoming deadlines for your coding problems and you’d like to come for advice or just work through the problems with the opportunity of support.
  • You’re looking for guidance on how to start coding from scratch.
  • We can offer help in the following languages: Python, Matlab, R, and general support in other programming languages.

This is a safe space to make mistakes, ask silly questions, and develop both your problem-solving skills and your confidence. Bring along any programming problems that you’re working on at the moment.

Coding Club takes place every Wednesday during term time 15:00 – 17:00 in Room 1.14 in the Physics Building. Book Now: https://bristol.ac.uk/students/your-studies/study-support/study-skills/workshops/#tags=677585220

posts.title: Summer and Career Updates
posts.content:
Ending my trip to Arizona in May 2023, I thought I would have a long summer holiday (school starts in late September for Bristol). However, I was wrong, somewhat gratefully, when my email inbox got a few acceptance letters.

So here is a post collecting some experiences that I did, and will be doing this academic year. They are mainly about mathematics and teaching, and I am looking forward to doing more of both in the future!

LMS Undergraduate Summer School

When I arrived in the UK, I immediately went to the University of Sheffield for the LMS Undergraduate Summer School. Which is my first time joining an undergraduate mathematics event in the UK. I met so many amazing people with different interests, and I really enjoyed the conversations: whether it was on maths, on our universities, or just chit-chatting!

In the 2 weeks of summer school, we did 6 mini-courses on different topics: such as probability, number theory, and algebraic geometry. I found out that there is a lot of algebra involved in mathematical physics (at least, in the way Dr. Alex Schenkel had taught it) and I enjoyed it a lot! We also did problem sessions, and there are various colloquiums to expose us to the frontiers of mathematics research!

I really enjoyed the time that I could intensely think about mathematics, and got in touch with different new concepts and play around with them. Especially in algebra, I learned about a categorical way to think about tensor products (as `machines’ that turn multi-linear maps into linear maps). And I learned to appreciate the categorical definition more!

Summer Research Project

After the summer school, I went back to Bristol to start my summer research project. I got an office shared with other research students! And I got a desk of my own too.

That being said, you usually would find me writing on the whiteboard in the computer room…

Anyways, the project is titled “Local Separators and Graphs”, and it is my first experience in full-time research. It is a project on combinatorics and a challenging one! I am writing more about this project, but the post is a WIP, so stay tuned!

Other Career Updates

I am now teaching more at Bristol! As some of you have noticed, there is now a “Teaching” tab on the navigation bar. Quite a lot of information is on there, so let me elaborate a little bit.

  • I am now returning as a course representative and a student advocate for Bristol Study Skills! I took on course rep in my first year, and student advocate in second. I will once again lead the Coding Club, so stay tuned for another post for more information!
  • I am now a Maths Cafe Leader! Maths cafes are optional support sessions for second-year students. As a leader, I aim to provide a space for students to talk about mathematics, and solve problems with them together. I am a leader for the course “Metric Spaces” for the first semester, and “Introduction to Geometry” next.

Since it is the start of the semester, I actually just started these roles! This is going to be a hectic year, but I will try to post updates of interesting things that I did.

posts.title: A few words on Study Abroad
posts.content:
Hi Everyone! I just started my final year at the University of Bristol. Since finishing my directed research project in May, I have not updated my blog. Part of the reason is that I am taking a (well-deserved) break over the summer.

However, there are so many interesting things that happened after the break – see my next few posts! For now, I just want to share my experience in Arizona and mention a few things that I find interesting. I guess most of the advice also applies to people who study abroad in general, not only in an exchange program.

As a report back to the University, I submitted a questionnaire here (obviously, some personal details are edited away), what I am going to say probably will repeat things from the document, as I am using it to refresh my memories anyway.

Sports and Well-being

People might have read my post on adapting again to my life in Arizona and noticed I posted a few photos of me hiking. I would really encourage other students studying abroad to work out a bit! Whether it is hiking, going to the gym, or just taking a stroll across campus, it is a really nice mental break from the intense subject experience.

I joined the F45 Training at the University of Arizona, which offers an unlimited number of classes throughout the year for a one-time payment of 90 USD, what a deal!

Differences between the US and UK

Back in Arizona, I hadn’t spent much time doing undergraduate math courses (I did some graduate-level math courses and presentations though). But still, there is a huge difference between classes in the US and UK. Most notably, it is way more common for professors to follow a certain textbook in the US. I know some lecturer in the UK does it too, but most of the time they write their own lecture notes.

When I was hanging out with other (postgraduate) classmates, I also found out that most US students, whether they are doing maths or not, have to take some sort of common maths sequence (of lessons) in the US. My classmates are TAs for those classes, where they go through high-school math (equations of lines, parabola, solving quadratic equations), and calculus (for science majors) again. There is nothing like this in the UK.

I don’t really know my feelings towards the maths sequence. On one hand, it is nice to know more about maths! But at the same time, I see different students stressed over those and really affects their GPA or progress to senior years on a subject not related to them. I wonder how do others feel about this?

Conclusion (that is completely irrelevant)

I guess for me, I haven’t experienced a lot of school life in Arizona. Because I spent all my time on math anyway, my major takeaway this year is to know more about doing a Ph.D. in the US. Talking to professors from different fields, and going to different conferences are eye-opening for me! Although I do not have much idea about my next steps, it is always nice to see and experience more.

posts.title: (A Draft of an) Expository Paper – Announcement
posts.content:
Hi everyone! I am happy to announce that I finish a draft version of an expository paper – Picard-Fuchs Equations and Cusp Forms! This will be used for part of my requirements for the MATH 492 Directed Research Unit at the University of Arizona.

I tried my best to put everything that I have learnt this semester into this paper. Although I am quite happy that I finished this, I do feel like I could do better. So, I decided to settle for a draft version of the paper, and decided that I will add details later in time – However, this is definitely wishful thinking…

This paper has the most important content all polished and good to go – in particular, the Sage code is what I am proud of the most! However, I feel like it is not very self-contained, as I feel like most topics can have better explanations.

Anyways, this also marks the end of my exchange year in Arizona! I am so glad that I met nice people: undergrads and PhD students, professors, and lecturers, that helped me become who I am today! Just want to say a big thank you to you all. And if you are reading this – thank you as well! Thank you for taking the time to read all this.

I will update more of my summer plans and what is happening next year on future blog posts.

~Ryan, 9 May 2023

posts.title: Shock and Adapting, Again
posts.content:
I still remember the mix of excitement and nervousness when I stepped foot in Bristol for the first time. Before the moment I received my study abroad offer (to the University of Arizona), I would never expect the feeling to hit me for the second time, but it sure did.

At Bristol: The Coding Club

Earlier in 2022, when I was at Bristol, I organized the coding club. Where I helped with all sorts of programming questions. It has been founded by two study skills advocates after realizing STEM students receive little to no continuous support when a course requires heavy coding. This had put a heavy toll on students that are not familiar with it.

As such, every Monday and Thursday, we have a 2-hour peer support session at one
of the study centres, where student advocates will help in answering all sorts of programming questions (Python, R, Java…) to the best of their abilities.

During the second semester, since there is a programming course which is compulsory
for all mathematics students, I signed up as an advocate who regularly helps with the Coding Club.

At one point, I decided to reach the lecturer of our programming course, and have him promote the Coding Club on our course website. And since then, there are more and more people coming to the study centre. At one point, I have to help 16 people with their math homework! In my opinion, this is a fun and valuable experience. I learned more about how to take an active role when organizing peer support activities. I also learned to lead and cultivate discussions throughout different sessions.

At Arizona: My Fall Semester

However, my life in the US is worlds apart. Although I had a rough idea of what will be coming ahead, experiencing the graduate courses, the homework, and the workplace culture first-hand would still put me in shock and huge pressure.

I feel way more challenged as the courses push me to the limits than I was in the UK. In the UK, my understanding comes from writing my notes and reading extra materials. But now, since the graduate courses have the content presented differently, I need to rely on homework and talking to professors to gain intuition into them.

I have only been here for a few months, but I can already imagine the struggles I will have as a potential US/UK PhD student in mathematics. Nevertheless, I am still glad that I can get a head start to experience the shock early.

Outside of Studying at Arizona

With this in mind, I ended up joining the Western Algebraic Geometry Symposium (WAGS) in Riverside, California. It turns out to be one of the most inspiring academic events I have joined. Despite not understanding 90% of the content, I managed to get a “feel” of Algebraic Geometry. I also found some topics that piqued my interest, and some kind-hearted PhD students explained their projects to me.  I also got to know some big names who are currently working on this hot and ever-expanding subject.

Outside of my studies, I also have leisure time as my other stream of inspiration. This year, I spent most of it on different sports, such as hiking, functional training and climbing. It let me realize how important it is to have undivided attention when pursuing a task, and how to listen to my body when things go south. Coincidentally, as a mathematician, I would also argue this is very important when tackling difficulties in research.

(This is a photo of me trying climbing and bouldering for the first time in Tucson.)

Conclusion

Compared to the UK, I would say I spent way more time in the US stumbling and exploring new and unknown territories. Moreover, I feel like I am a step closer to what mathematical research really is: pushing boundaries with careful justifications. As time goes on, I feel like I am slowly but surely adapting to the working style. My trip to the US definitely pushed my boundaries in understanding and practising mathematics. I sincerely hope the spring semester will be as fruitful as the fall one!

posts.title: Time Management and Baking
posts.content:
Since moving into my newly rented house from my student halls, I had to adapt to the new environment. Living and knowing flatmates that I haven’t seen before, reorganizing a lot of daily necessities and activities… etc. Although it was a challenging experience for me, I enjoy the process a lot. Specifically, I started to develop an interest in baking.

Our kitchen in the rented house is quite large, which means there is a lot of equipment for me to use and sharpen my cooking skills. And when at weekends where I had some spare time, I tried to find some recipes online, buy the ingredients at a store, and bake them the week after.

The first few times of baking is definitely challenging, sometimes I made a real mess and ended up spending more time cleaning than cooking! But after a few trials and errors, I started to get the hang of it. Specifically, I learnt to wash and clean different utensils as you go along and prepare ahead for the next steps in a more natural way. In the end, I would say I am quite satisfied with the result.

I think the process of baking hinted at some lessons about managing my time in university life. There are moments where you must multitask, such as waiting for the dough to rest and preparing the fillings, and it is best to plan ahead and be clear on what you are about to do! This is also true in studying: where sometimes you have to think about the tools or the resources that you will need before starting a project.

But most importantly, it is always good to experiment with different strategies and methods, just as you would in making a cake! Chances are you probably will not be satisfied with your first result. After learning this lesson, I feel more motivated in trying different things regarding my life and studies.

posts.title: MAT & TMUA 2021: Tips and Advice
posts.content:
The following article written by me is posted on the EasyA Discord group, I think it would be better if I post it here! Also, I really want more people to know more about EasyA, so I pasted an ad-like message at the bottom introducing them.

Hey all! It is MAT tomorrow (and TMUA the day after), I guess everyone is quite nervous about it. As a student who took the MAT before, I just want to offer some tips and advice that might help! These strategies might not work for anyone, but here are some of them I think test-preppers can take some references on:

0️⃣MAT is hard, TMUA is hard, math is hard!

Firstly, I really want to congratulate you guys on making it towards the end of an exam prep period. It is no easy task to surround yourself with so many difficult questions for such a long time.⏲️ Each question requires some serious thinking, and it is frustrating when the results don’t click! But don’t worry, those admission tests are designed like that: the examiners want to see you struggle, and want to stretch your limits😈. So don’t be let down because you hadn’t got any clue about a question! Remember, the mean score of applicants who were made an Oxford offer could be as low as 60/100 in MAT, and you never know when the question is getting exceptionally hard!😫

1️⃣Golden Rule: ⭐Don’t panic!⭐

This is much easier said than done, it will affect your university applications by a lot, and you have prepared so much, so it is completely normal to feel tense. Especially when you are in an exam hall: all the people are focused and looking at their paper ferociously, it is easy to fall into a state of panic after starting. One thing that will be nice to remember, is that if you are panicking on a question, then probably the people around you do too. So you are not alone in this sense. Think about what you had practised, skip the question if necessary and keep following your strategy in doing the question!

2️⃣Develop a strategy📰

By now, you probably had practised a few papers and know that the marking scheme is: 4×10 MCs + 15×4 Long Questions that make a total of 100 marks in 150 minutes. Think about approximately how long you are spending on each question. I made an approximate timetable📝 before I start working (approx. half an hour in 5 MCs, then 20 minutes in each long question), then follow it throughout. Think about will you check your work at all or the end of your question? Or after completing as much as you could? It is okay either way, but make sure you are clear about what to do, so you make full use of your time!

3️⃣Work quickly but write a lot!✏️

The time limit for MAT is especially harsh, once you laid your eyes on a question you almost had to start right away in order to get the answer. For every question (especially long questions), my strategy is to write as many things as possible when I could think of any. Especially in long questions, if you don’t write any of your thoughts down, then the markers are not going to know your thinking process😖! Even if your thought process is wrong, there is a very high chance to get partial credit by noting down any pattern that emerges from the question. Be confident! Don’t be afraid to make any mistakes!

4️⃣Claim what you are going to do.🔊

You won’t believe how useful it is to have phrases like “comparing coefficients in the polynomial…”, “solving the simultaneous equations…”, “rearranging…”, “using the substitution…” weaved into your answer! It makes your presentation way clearer than just writing one line and then the other. This is quite hard to do especially you are panicking, but if you can realize what you are doing by writing such phrases, it can make your answers less error-prone✔️!

5️⃣Write Clearly and legibly.

You all probably have heard from others how important handwriting is, so I am not going to elaborate a lot here🥱. But one common misconception is that in Multiple choice questions (MCQs) you can just write in a language that only you understands. Although you don’t have to write phrases to guide the markers, it would still be a good thing to do if you can write as if you are answering a long question (if you have the time), again, this highly reduced the likeliness of making a careless mistake, since you are so clear with your work!

6️⃣Double-check your workings!🧐

It is really up to different people on when they will check their workings. For me, after a painful expansion of brackets or taking out minus signs, I always look twice and stop for a few seconds to make sure that I am doing the right thing. Some might do that after they are stuck or after they finish a whole (sub-)question. Those strategies are fine as well👍! There is no one successful way, but just do the way that you are most comfortable with.

7️⃣Sleep Well, eat your breakfast!🥣

It is very important to have some energy before tackling such a hard paper⚡! But of course, it is definitely not the case that everyone can just sleep once they lay down on their bed, especially before an exam day like this😪. So, maybe read something, do something that you like before sleep, talk to friends, play some games, make yourself at ease the night before😸! And of course, check your alarm, make yourself feel comfortable after you wake up, enjoy the day, and enjoy the paper!

🏁Final words

There are only 14 questions in MAT that you need to attempt, so sometimes luck plays a role here in whether the light bulb in your head💡 suddenly clicks. Your performance is only an indicator of your ability, but it is certainly not what DESCRIBES your abilities. No matter how the exam turned out, I am sure all of you reading this had put a lot of effort into it, and you should be proud of yourself🥺! To all of the candidates here, I wish you could do your very best, and best of luck💪! Do feel free if you have any questions or need any help, I will try my best to help and provide support if you need to.

A Note on EasyA

EasyA is an organization that helps to close the attainment gap for students by providing free math volunteer services online. I would really recommend anyone who wants to have a big impact on school students’ lives to get involved! You tutor via text on your phone, so if you’re free for just 10 mins you can literally just go online and start helping out! ⏰ It literally takes 1 minute to get started as a tutor: https://lnkd.in/gUdUGgwU

Here is a description of EasyA, courtesy to Phil Kwok and Dom Kwok for getting me into the tutoring team!

Stuck on a tricky maths question? Nobody to ask for help? EasyA is a FREE mobile app that allows you to get help from other expert student tutors who’ve recently been through the exams you’re studying for – all in minutes. Download it now on iOS/Android here: https://lnkd.in/gaYUurW9 You can connect with someone who can help in 3 simple steps:

1. Take a pic of your question

2. Send it

3. Connect with a tutor who can help you through it!

The EasyA Discord Group also offer completely free help and service if you want other non-academic advice such as study skills and university application advice! Join by clicking the invite link here: https://discord.com/invite/jUn8bahCJx

posts.title: Course Review: “Responsive Web Design” on freeCodeCamp.org
posts.content:
How could a man unable to draw well got a certificate in web design?

As a student who is passionate about presenting different ideas, whether academic or not, I think there is increasing importance on learning how technology can help me. One idea that comes up to me is learning about website architecture. Although I am currently using WordPress, which provides me with a useful template, I still feel that it is crucial to learn the theory behind designing a website.

I was a bit hesitant before starting to work on this, as I knew my art and aesthetic sense is as terrible as it is… and I am pretty afraid that it might affect my ability to comprehend different visual elements in a webpage.

After taking the course, needless to say, I had understood more about how to interpret each visual style that is present in a website by reading its code. It teaches the basics of different elements on a website with the usage of HTML5 and CSS. It is a course heavily focus on visual design, including topics like increasing accessibility in a website, arranging different elements, and the new but powerful CSS flexbox.

I like the coding environment presented in the course, and since it is completely free (unlike other competitors which require a paid service often), I think that the content covered is vast and sufficient compared to other coding courses. However, it is quite a bit of an overestimate to say that it contains 300 hours of content (as stated in the certificate). Consider how I finished the course under 3 weeks… but maybe it is the projects / final assignments that take up most of the time, I will explain that later.

The course contains numerous programming “challenges” that let you solve to gain an understanding of a subject. Each unit has about 20 of them. Disappointingly, these “challenges” usually contain only 1 to 2 lines of code, with very explicit instructions, so most of the time it is just reading comprehension for me. However, some of it might be challenging for coding newbies. So sometimes I am feeling that I am overqualified for the certificate.

After the challenges, there are 5 final tasks to finish to claim the certification. To finish the task, you must write a website, fulfilling the user stories set by the questions, and pass all the tests on a test checker.  For each task, you can see the test checker’s result and show what you did wrong. You also have an example website (which pass all the tests) for you to refer to. I like both of the features, it makes website design seems less boring and much more creative, it also can boost you to design a more appealing website if you are able.

I understand that most of our fellow learners here would want to write a beautiful website, but sadly I am running out of time when I was studying for this certificate. It is September, and I had to prepare my materials back for my uni, and as mentioned, I am also not good with visual arts. I ended up writing a minimal example with the least material while passing all the tests. And that gives me a huge time save, I don’t know whether this is a good thing or not, but it passes all the tests so I don’t have a lot to say about it.

Criticisms aside, the content still makes me confident in the basics of designing a website. Does it make me think it is an artsy thing? Maybe, that’s why it is a 3.5/5 from me, but I would recommend this course to people who have absolutely no programming experience and want to learn a new skill. And most importantly, it is completely free! Just go to freecodecamp.org and get started!

posts.title: Course Review: “Introduction to Complex Analysis” on Coursera
posts.content:
The following article is a review I wrote for the online course “Introduction to Complex Analysis”, organized by Dr Petra Bonfert-Taylor and Wesleyan University, and published on Coursera.

This course contains an overview of manipulation in complex numbers at a second-year undergraduate level. Various techniques, such as visualizing mappings, solving integrals, and manipulating series in complex numbers are introduced. The course also goes through some of the application of a few crucial theorems, such as Cauchy-Riemann Equations, Cauchy’s Theorem and Cauchy Integral Formula.

8 weeks ago, I started this course with a knowledge of some very basic real analysis (the epsilon-delta definition of convergence, differentiation, and Riemann integration). As a major in mathematics, I found this course refreshing and a pleasure to take. Dr Taylor’s voice was engaging, and the lecture notes were self-contained and well-explained.

One remarkable feature that I want to highlight is the coursework component. It consisted of graded quizzes with multiple choices, tick boxes, and some short fill in the blanks. There were also graded peer assignments once per 2 weeks, this made sure that our answers produced are readable by other people. I found the difficulty of the coursework very appropriate: it was deliberately not straightforward, and you must be careful while applying different theorems and concepts that were taught in the lessons. The peer-graded assignment also emphasized communicating mathematics carefully, with clearly given guidance and appropriate suggestions from other learners, it was a very well thought out part of the course.

The course was very enjoyable on its own. But certain features could be more well-polished. Overall, this feels like a course for applied mathematicians. Heavy focus is put on and applying the results. However, with a little bit of generalization and more discussions of proofs and their logic behind them, it can benefit more pure mathematicians that are interested in the subject. Similarly, I think the assignments (especially the peer-graded ones) can be more proof-centric, with more videos explaining the sketch of proof in more detail. Therefore, the course can aim for a balance between applied and pure content, which would in turn benefit more learners.

Moreover, even with the addition of Residue Calculus, I still think that more content can be added to the course. It currently contains topics such as Solving Real-valued Integrals, Understanding the Mandelbrot set, etc. But more applied topics, such as introducing the idea of the harmonic equation in liquid flow or heat flow using polar coordinate might be more inspiring and make the course more fulfilling.

Lastly, I found Week 5 (The first week that introduces complex integration) particularly challenging. I think I spent twice the time revising it compared to other units in this course. Therefore I think it will be better to add new content and let the whole course be 12-week long or so.

Overall, I enjoy this course a lot, and I will recommend anyone who has an interest in Complex numbers and have 1-2 years of experience in university STEM subjects.

posts.title: Mathematics Competitions in High School
posts.content:
I studied high school in Hong Kong with Physics, Chemistry and “Further Mathematics” (M2 in HKDSE) as electives. So I was probably the most generic “scientist nerdy” type of people you would find in school, not particularly able or whatsoever. However, I did have an immense interest in mathematics, especially after experiencing outside lessons such as EPYMT. 

That said, I did not participate in any mathematics competition during high school, nor I participated in any kind of competition training. This might seem odd, but even now, I am still convinced that I made the right decision by not participating in any at that time. The idea of constantly participating in mathematics competition is doing more harm than good for me.

Schoolwork and Pressure

The current Hong Kong’s education system (the HKDSE) is infamous for its competitiveness and difficulty. Students are, if not obligated, expected to cram things in 3 years. For comparison, this is equivalent to absorbing everything you learn in GCSE and A-Levels while having a year less. We have had extra lessons in the summer holidays, after school, only to do a few more practice papers and tests (and my secondary school is already known for not pushing students too hard).

That means after a day’s work you will be exhausted, and given how much thinking and brainpower you would need for mathematics competition questions, it wasn’t the best idea for me to stumble into these. Besides, I was already participating in different pre-university math classes and reading math books already, which I would argue to be more effective.

The idea behind Math Competitions

Some people might say I am just being lazy and don’t want to work harder. While it might be true that I can achieve more, I still don’t think mathematics competitions would be the right way. To be honest, I think having participated in a competition doesn’t help very much in studying mathematics as one could have expected. 

This Answer from Quora made a point that I agree with: although the answer is specifically talking about the International Mathematics Olympiad (IMO), I think it applies to all mathematics competition at a high school level. The answer to a question requires a trick and/or a key observation to get through, and it could get quite frustrating when you try your best, but you don’t succeed. (I have included a reference here, please tell me that I am funny)

Anyways, doing mathematics as a university major is more than the skills you need in a competition. Sure, practicing would help you in finding patterns and identifying ideas. But more importantly, doing mathematics requires the ability to invent new ideas, communicate, and then present. This can only be trained by researching and presenting, in my opinion, since you don’t have a strict time limit by then, and can explore as deep as you like. I had experienced this full learning cycle during my Mathematical Investigation Workshop, and I can conclude that it is nothing like competition training.

My findings can be best summarized by a quote from the answer I mentioned:

The plight of the IMO Olympian is like that of a child at Easter Egg hunts, where they have grown used to finding pretty eggs laid out previously by adults, and then when they grow up and come to a large grassy field, they are frustrated, because no matter how hard they try they can’t find a single egg in the bushes —because in the real world of mathematics, there is no adult planting pretty eggs for them to find.

Epilogue/Disclaimer

I am not saying Competition mathematics is not a good activity for high school student, I think you are confident enough, things would turn out great for you and you will have the bragging rights too! However, I want to emphasize that mathematics competitions are quite different from mathematics itself, and not all good mathematicians are good competition problem-solver, vice versa.

After saying this much, I want to declare that I am also on a university mathematics competition training, so that’s why I have a little bit of experience of what high school students are experiencing in mathematical competitions.

Also, starting from now on, I would post some explanations of competitions problems here, showing as much thought process that I had gone through as possible.

posts.title: University Experience – Being a Course Representative
posts.content:
My secondary school life is very academic-intensive and fruitful. However, upon reviewing my personal profile at my last year, I notice that I did not participate in a lot of competition and projects…

So the main reason is probably that there were so many people that are much stronger than me academically, so I never really got the chance. In mathematics, I am not that keen on participating in competition anyways (maybe more on that on a blog post later), and there were much fewer project opportunities compared to other applied science subject, such as Biology (which I am notoriously bad at).

…and I feel like there is a need for a change.

To be honest, upon entering the University of Bristol, (negatively speaking) I was quite desperate to convince myself that I indeed have some value in the School of Mathematics, and that’s why I have been looking for different roles that I can take and to experience something new, something that I can’t get in my Secondary school.

Consequently, one of my goals I set for myself would be improving my skills as an effective communicator. Therefore, I had nominated myself into various experience and volunteering organized by the University of Bristol Students’​ Union. This also comes with a purpose to know how to school operates as a democratic system, and how are students’ voice represented.

I attended different meetings with senior members of the staff and other course rep and discussed various feedback from other coursemates. During the process, I also learnt to collect opinions using different social media: from creating and handing out google forms in WhatsApp chat, to compiling the statistics in excel and report back to the staff, I learnt a lot while being a middle man for two paramount bodies in the University.

After this year, this kind of boosted my confidence in various aspect. It is very rewarding to see that you can make a change in the University’s decision, even very minimally. I will continue to pursue related representative (even a Faculty representative next year?), and aim to help and support all of the student in my course as fullest as possible. So if you are a student studying the same course with me reading this, remember to give me some support! Haha.

posts.title: My Experience: EPYMT
posts.content:
While planning for university options in Grade 11 (Form 5 in HK), although I had a clear idea of pursuing mathematics, I never actually got a taste of what university (studying) life is. With curiosity and no knowledge of any topics whatsoever, I stumbled into this course. Little did I know it will become one of the most influential mathematical events to me.

Two courses are offered to me during this programme: “Understanding Non-Euclidean Geometry” in July, and “Number Theory and Cryptography” in August. Both courses took place at the campus of CUHK, with lectures (09:30-12:00), and tutorials (13:00-16:15) for 10 days, using only 3 weeks per course. At the end of each week, there would be a test, with a final exam at the end of the whole course. Grades and scholarships will be awarded according to them.

No need to say, this was a very high-intensity training for me, especially during the non-Euclidean Geometry part, where knowledge about different proofing techniques and mathematical object is already assumed. I had to extract information from the lecture using the 1-hour lunchtime and apply it during our tutorial, where the teaching assistants would demonstrate follow-up question and assign different homework that prepared us for the quiz.

Nevertheless, by absorbing all the content rapidly, I realized I enjoyed the two courses a lot. From Mobius transformation to models of hyperbolic geometry, from the Chinese remainder theorem to the RSA encryption algorithm, the course acted as a huge expository talk for different branches of mathematics. The teaching assistant’s comment and other guest lectures in the program also helped me a lot in consolidating and understanding mathematics in general.

As a result, I am awarded the “Excellence Performance Award” in the course at the Number Theory course in August, and completed the course with a scholarship. It enormously boosted my confidence in university mathematics.

~ Ryan, 21 May 2021
